# Which side of the frame did the lone walker come from?

## Short answer

**They would have entered the shot from the BOTTOM of the frame** — out of the
near foreground, closest to the camera — and walked away from the viewer, up
into the plaza. They would not have come in from the left side, the right side,
or the top.

More precisely: back-projecting their line of travel takes them out through the
bottom edge of the picture roughly a third of the way across from the left
(i.e. bottom, just left of centre, near the big ornate lamp standard and the
giant wire Christmas bauble in the foreground).

## Who the person is

The figure in question is the solitary pedestrian standing almost exactly at the
centre of the picture (about 49% across, 45% down), out on the open snow-covered
plaza between the cream-coloured corner building on the left and the row of
steel bollards on the upper right. They are the only person in that part of the
frame who is on their own — everyone else nearby is in a pair, a family group,
or a standing cluster. They wear a dark hat, a long light grey/oatmeal coat with
a black scarf dark at the collar and hanging down the side, a dark
maroon-brown skirt below the coat hem, a black shoulder bag, and black shoes.

## Why the answer is "bottom"

**1. We are looking at this person's back, not their front.**
At this magnification their whole head reads as one dark mass — hat plus the
back of the head — with no face. I checked that numerically rather than by eye:
every pixel in the head is colour-neutral, with red-minus-blue values of only
+3 to +13, the same as the surrounding snow. By comparison, people in this same
photograph who are walking *towards* the camera — for instance the couple in the
orange knit hat and olive parka lower down the frame — show unmistakably warm
skin pixels, red-minus-blue of +40 and higher. There is no skin anywhere on this
figure's head. The camera is therefore behind them.

**2. Having your back to this camera means walking towards the top of the frame.**
The photo is taken from a high window looking down on the square, so the scene
recedes towards the top of the image. Someone with their back to the lens is
travelling away from the viewer, i.e. up the frame. Run that backwards and they
must have come from the near foreground, which is the bottom edge.

**3. Their heading is close to straight away, not sideways.**
Several independent checks agree:
- The body is seen back-on, not in profile. The coat measures about 15 px wide,
  which at the scale of this part of the image is roughly 0.44 m — a shoulder
  width. A true side-on profile would be narrower, around 0.3 m.
- The head sits centred over the shoulders and the shoulder line runs almost
  horizontally across the image, which is the signature of a body facing
  directly up or down the frame.
- The two feet are separated mainly side-to-side (about 9 px, ~0.26 m) and
  barely at all in depth. Somebody striding across the frame would show a long
  horizontal foot separation of roughly a full stride; this is the compact
  foot placement of someone moving away from the camera.
- The torso is essentially upright. Allowing for the slight convergence of true
  verticals in this image (measured from two lamp posts, which lean about
  0.035 and 0.07 px sideways per px of height, putting the vertical vanishing
  point far below the frame at roughly x = 140), the head sits only about 1 px
  off plumb over the feet — no meaningful sideways lean.

**4. There is a small rightward drift, and it does not change the answer.**
The outer point of the right shoulder sits about 2 px lower in the image than
the outer point of the left shoulder. Only about 0.6 px of that is explained by
the slight roll of the camera, so the right shoulder is genuinely a little
closer to the lens. That means the body is turned by roughly 10 degrees towards
the upper right — so the person is walking away from the camera and very
slightly to the right, heading in the general direction of the bollards and the
street running up to the top right.

Projecting that heading backwards through the plaza takes them down the frame
and slightly to the left, crossing the bottom edge at around x = 350 of 1023.
I also tested the extremes of the uncertainty: even a 30-degree rightward or a
substantial leftward heading still puts the exit point inside the bottom edge.
Only if they were walking nearly sideways across the frame — which the back-on
silhouette rules out — would they have come from a left or right edge.

## Stated plainly

If this were a video clip, the woman in the grey coat, black scarf and black
shoes would have walked into shot from the **bottom edge of the frame**, out of
the foreground nearest the camera and slightly left of centre, and then
continued directly away from the viewer, deeper into the snowy square towards
the top of the picture.

## Confidence

High on the main point — the absence of any skin tone on the head, the back-on
silhouette width, and the compact, laterally-separated feet all say the same
thing: she is walking away from the camera, so she entered from the near/bottom
edge, not from a side. The genuinely uncertain part is only the small lateral
